teaser.text: Admiral Group is a UK-founded company that sells insurance and lends money, so its business begins with promises about future protection or repayments. To understand how money comes in and goes out, follow it from the customer, through premium or loan, to claims, costs, funding and profit.

blocks.heading: What drives Admiral's bear, base and bull cases?

paragraphs.text: The bear case starts at £710m, falls to £660m and then £650m because claims inflation and competition prevent repricing from improving margins. UK Motor claims costs were 7% higher year on year in Q2 2026. The bull case starts at £950m, then reaches £1,050m and £1,150m as customer growth and profitable scaling in Europe, MoreThan, Flock and Admiral Money compound. UK risks rose to 9.58m from 8.80m, while Flock was acquired for £76.4m cash. The forecast excludes separate benefits from reserve releases and acquisition accounting because 2025 profit included £386.4m of releases.

blocks.heading: How does Admiral turn insurance and lending into shareholder returns?

paragraphs.text: The insurer holds financial assets to meet future claims and regulatory capital needs. Premium receipts, claim payments, investment purchases and sales, and loans advanced to customers therefore move cash without mapping neatly onto ordinary operating profit. Free cash flow, free-cash-flow yield and the current ratio can consequently mislead.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Admiral's earnings?

paragraphs.text: The first lens is the price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E. It says how much investors pay for each pound of profit, while a forward P/E uses an estimate of future profit. Imagine paying £17 for a shop that earned £1 last year but is expected to earn £1.25 next year. The lower forward multiple is attractive only if that extra profit arrives.

dividend.opening: Admiral targets a normal dividend of 65% of post-tax profit, with forecast dividends per share ranging from £0.90 to £2.00 across the bear and bull cases. Cash coverage is not a clean retail-style test: Admiral's capital needs, growth plans and insurance cash flows affect distributions.
dividend.closing: The full Admiral memo also explains its business, management choices, rivals and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does Admiral pay per share?

paragraphs.text: Dividends follow Admiral's stated 65% ordinary payout policy. Base DPS rises from £1.43 to £1.52 and £1.60 as earnings recover. The bear case falls from £1.10 to £0.95 and £0.90; the bull case rises from £1.55 to £1.80 and £2.00. That spread reflects the company's uneven DPS record, which ranged from £0.734 to £1.587 in the supplied history.

blocks.heading: Does Admiral's cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: The table shows that Admiral’s largest distributions included cash released by the Penguin sale. That rewarded shareholders immediately, but it left future expansion dependent on later profits or further asset sales. In 2025, Admiral kept only £30.2 million, compared with £281.8 million in 2024, so less of that year’s profit remained available to build the business.

paragraphs.text: Management targets a normal dividend of 65% of post-tax profit, subject to capital needs and growth. The announced buyback is capped at £45.0m through 31 December 2026.

H2 2026 is the first test: lower UK Motor reinsurance charges and rate increases should support profit. UK Motor claims costs were 7% higher year on year in Q2 2026. Flock’s £76.4m cash acquisition in May 2026 must turn commercial fleet growth into profitable policies. The internal capital-model application will test capital headroom and future distributions.

blocks.heading: What is Admiral's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: Dividends and buybacks are two ways profit reaches shareholders. A dividend pays cash directly; a buyback uses company money to repurchase and cancel shares, leaving the remaining owners with a larger percentage of the business. In H1 2026, Admiral declared a 70.5p dividend and a £45 million buyback. Its solvency ratio was 190% after those payments, showing capital headroom but not removing risk.
